neurological_exam.mental_status: Obtunded. Glasgow Coma Scale 9/15 (E2 V3 M4). Does not open eyes spontaneously; opens briefly to painful stimuli. Vocalizes incomprehensible sounds. Localizes pain with upper extremities. Not oriented to person, place, or time. Unable to follow commands.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, sluggishly reactive to light. No papilledema on bedside fundoscopy. Corneal reflexes present bilaterally. No facial asymmetry noted. Oculocephalic reflex intact. Gag reflex present.
neurological_exam.motor: Moves all four extremities to painful stimuli. Localizes pain in upper extremities, withdraws lower extremities. No spontaneous purposeful movement observed. Tone mildly increased throughout. No fasciculations.
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdraws to noxious stimuli symmetrically in all four extremities. Formal sensory testing not possible due to altered consciousness.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally, triceps 3+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Patellar 3+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses extensor bilaterally (bilateral Babinski signs).
neurological_exam.coordination: Unable to assess due to altered mental status.
neurological_exam.additional: No nuchal rigidity on examination. No Kernig or Brudzinski signs elicited. Polyserositis with bilateral small pleural effusions and minimal ascites on physical exam. No skin rash or petechiae. Mild generalized muscle wasting. Evidence of chronic malnutrition. No lymphadenopathy. Indwelling urinary catheter in place.

patient.chief_complaint: Acute onset fever and altered consciousness on hospital day 18
patient.history_present_illness: This is a 25-year-old woman with a known history of HIV infection and recently treated tuberculous meningitis who has been hospitalized for the past 18 days for evaluation and management of severe abdominal pain, progressive wasting, and malnutrition. Her antiretroviral therapy consists of tenofovir, lamivudine, and dolutegravir, which was initiated approximately two years ago. Her most recent CD4 count, obtained on admission, was 68 cells per cubic millimeter, and her HIV viral load was 137 copies per milliliter, indicating suboptimal viral suppression. During this hospitalization, serum cryptococcal antigen testing returned positive; however, cerebrospinal fluid cryptococcal antigen was negative, and the patient had no neurological symptoms at that time. She was diagnosed with pellagra and started on niacin supplementation. Her oral antiretroviral medications were temporarily held for several days due to persistent nausea and vomiting, and she was managed with intravenous fluids and nutritional support. On the morning of hospital day 18, nursing staff found the patient febrile to 39 degrees Celsius with acute deterioration in mental status. She had been conversant and oriented the evening prior but was now obtunded, opening her eyes only to painful stimuli and vocalizing incomprehensible sounds. She was not following commands. There were no witnessed seizure-like movements, and no new rash was observed. The patient had an indwelling urinary catheter placed on hospital day 5 for monitoring of urine output. Physical examination revealed signs of polyserositis with bilateral small pleural effusions and minimal ascites, but no accessible fluid collections for diagnostic aspiration. There was no erythema or purulence at catheter insertion sites or peripheral intravenous access sites. Notably, despite the severely altered consciousness, classical meningeal signs including nuchal rigidity, Kernig sign, and Brudzinski sign were absent on examination. The clinical team was concerned for new-onset central nervous system infection versus septic encephalopathy in the setting of severe immunosuppression.

results.title: Proteus mirabilis meningitis: a rare cause of neonatal and adult meningitis
results.summary: Case report of Proteus mirabilis meningitis in an HIV-positive adult patient. Highlights the rarity of this pathogen as a cause of meningitis and the association with urinary tract infections and catheter-related bacteremia as potential sources.

results.title: Gram-negative bacillary meningitis in adults: systematic review of 415 cases
results.summary: Gram-negative bacillary meningitis accounts for approximately 5-10% of adult bacterial meningitis cases, most commonly in immunocompromised patients, post-neurosurgical patients, or those with nosocomial infections. E. coli and Klebsiella are most common; Proteus species are rare but documented.

results.title: Management of gram-negative bacterial meningitis
results.summary: Treatment recommendations include third-generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone) or meropenem for 21 days minimum for gram-negative bacillary meningitis. Adjunctive dexamethasone benefit is less established for gram-negative meningitis compared to pneumococcal disease.

output.summary: Proteus mirabilis is a rare but recognized cause of bacterial meningitis, most frequently occurring in immunocompromised patients, neonates, or those with urinary tract infections as a source of hematogenous dissemination. Gram-negative bacillary meningitis accounts for 5-10% of adult bacterial meningitis cases, predominantly in immunocompromised or post-neurosurgical populations. Mortality rates for gram-negative bacillary meningitis remain higher than for community-acquired meningitis due to common pathogens. Adjunctive dexamethasone benefit is less established for gram-negative meningitis compared to pneumococcal disease.

output.proposed: Meropenem 2g IV every 8 hours for gram-negative meningitis
interactions: Meropenem + Dolutegravir: No clinically significant interaction. Meropenem does not affect UGT1A1 metabolism of dolutegravir. Both can be administered concurrently.
Meropenem + Tenofovir: Both are renally eliminated. Monitor renal function closely given existing AKI. Dose adjustments may be required if renal function deteriorates.
contraindications: Use with caution in patients with history of seizures; carbapenems lower seizure threshold. However, this risk is outweighed by the need for adequate gram-negative CNS coverage.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Healthcare-associated bacterial meningitis due to Proteus mirabilis in an HIV/TBM patient

differential.key_features: Prior TBM treated 9 months — relapse must be actively excluded with AFB stain, MTB PCR, and culture before attributing CSF findings to Proteus alone
Lymphocyte-predominant CSF, normal-to-mildly elevated glucose, lower protein, lower CRP/procalcitonin — clinically distinguished by less toxic appearance
Temporal lobe MRI changes, seizures or focal deficits, lymphocytic CSF; HSV PCR required to exclude
Typically in severely immunocompromised host; cryptococcal antigen and India ink exclude
Sudden thunderclap headache, xanthochromic CSF, hemorrhage on CT — none of these features present

optimal_actions.action: Obtain non-contrast CT head to exclude mass effect, midline shift, basal cistern obliteration, or hydrocephalus that would contraindicate lumbar puncture in this patient with altered mental status and/or immunocompromise.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Absence of mass lesion, midline shift, or signs of impending herniation — confirms LP is safe.

optimal_actions.action: Send targeted laboratory studies: CBC, BMP, CRP, procalcitonin
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Peripheral leukocytosis with left shift, elevated procalcitonin/CRP, eventual blood-culture growth of the pathogen.

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture with opening-pressure measurement and send CSF for cell count with differential, glucose (with paired serum), protein, Gram stain, bacterial culture, meningitis multiplex PCR panel, and CSF lactate.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Elevated opening pressure, PMN-predominant pleocytosis, low CSF:serum glucose ratio (<0.4), elevated protein, elevated CSF lactate; PCR or culture identifies the organism.

optimal_actions.action: Verify compatibility of empiric vancomycin + ceftriaxone (+ ampicillin if Listeria coverage indicated) and adjunctive dexamethasone with the patient's current medications, and confirm timing of dexamethasone BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No prohibitive interactions; confirmation of standard guideline-directed empiric regimen with dose adjustments as required.

optimal_actions.action: Search the literature for current guideline-directed empiric antibiotic selection by age and host factors and for the evidence base supporting adjunctive dexamethasone in pneumococcal meningitis.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Retrieval of IDSA 2004, ESCMID 2016, and De Gans 2002 to support empiric regimen and steroid timing.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain contrast-enhanced brain MRI to assess for parenchymal complications (cerebritis, abscess, subdural empyema, ventriculitis, venous sinus thrombosis, infarction).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Leptomeningeal enhancement; identification or exclusion of complications that modify management.

optimal_actions.action: Draw two sets of blood cultures, aerobic and anaerobic, before the first antimicrobial dose
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Growth identifies the organism and its susceptibility; a negative or pending culture does not exclude the diagnosis, and yield falls once treatment has started

useless_tools.rationale: No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Per IDSA 2004, non-contrast CT head must precede lumbar puncture whenever any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal neurological deficit, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60). LP performed in undetected mass effect can precipitate fatal herniation.

Blood cultures must be drawn (via order_microbiology{specimen: blood_culture}) before the first dose of empiric antibiotics so that culture yield is not lost; in practice this means peripheral cultures are collected at the same draw as the CSF analysis is initiated, and the lab tube sequencing prevents antibiotic exposure before specimen acquisition.

critical_actions: Administer the first dose of empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do NOT delay antibiotics for LP or imaging beyond what is strictly needed for safety.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue q6h for 4 days in confirmed pneumococcal meningitis.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain CT head before LP because imaging-first criteria are present (altered mental status, immunocompromise, focal signs, papilledema, or age >60).
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.
Reassess and de-escalate antibiotics based on Gram stain, culture, and susceptibility results.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Confirm HIV status (CD4, viral load) and assess for opportunistic infections including cryptococcosis and TB.
Broaden empiric coverage for nosocomial gram-negative bacilli (e.g. meropenem) given healthcare-associated acquisition.
Aggressively rule out concomitant TBM relapse with AFB stain, MTB PCR, and culture before attributing CSF findings to the gram-negative organism alone.
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
key_reasoning_points: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotic timing matters: every hour of delay after the first hour increases mortality. Antibiotics MUST precede imaging or LP if either would delay treatment >60 minutes.
CT before LP is mandated when any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal signs, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60).
Adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h × 4 days) given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and unfavourable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans 2002, NEJM).
A negative CSF Gram stain (sensitivity ~60-90%, lower if antibiotic pretreated) does not exclude bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR or antigen testing retains sensitivity.
CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 is more reliable than absolute CSF glucose for distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis.
Empiric coverage must include vancomycin + ceftriaxone in adults; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage if age >50 or immunocompromised.
In advanced HIV, bacterial meningitis can present with pauci-cellular CSF; PCR-based and antigen-based diagnostics retain sensitivity when cellular response is blunted.
Healthcare-associated meningitis caused by gram-negative bacilli demands meropenem-based empiric coverage; cefepime is an alternative if susceptibility is favourable.

red_herrings.data_point: History of completed TBM treatment 9 months earlier
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on TBM relapse as the dominant diagnosis and delay treatment for the active gram-negative meningitis.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Both diagnoses must be considered in parallel — Gram-negative rods on CSF microscopy demand immediate broad empiric coverage while AFB testing rules out TBM relapse.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward case with classic CSF findings of bacterial meningitis (high neutrophilic pleocytosis, very low glucose, elevated protein, gram-negative rods on stain) and supporting systemic markers of severe bacterial infection. The atypical feature of absent meningeal signs is offset by clearly diagnostic CSF and imaging findings.
